rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading takes Moses to deny Pharaoh’s claimed favor: raising him was no kindness because Pharaoh enslaved Moses’ people and thereby canceled the good deed.
rows.anchor: إنكار لأصل النعمة عليه لمكان تعبيده بني إسرائيل كأنه يقول إن تربيتك لي ليست نعمة يمن بها علي لأنك عبدت قومي فأحبطت به عملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although this reading seems closer than the preceding one, the author says it fails: enslaving Israel did not change the reality of Pharaoh’s kindness in raising Moses as an infant.
rows.anchor: هذا الجواب غير تام معنى فإن تعبيده لبني إسرائيل لا يغير حقيقة ما له من الصنيعة عند موسى في تربيته وليدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading makes Moses’ upbringing a consequence of Pharaoh’s oppression: enslavement forced his mother to cast him into the river, where Pharaoh found and raised him, so it was no favor.
rows.anchor: هذه النعمة التي تمن بها علي من التربية إنما سببه ظلمك بني إسرائيل بتعبيدهم فاضطرت أمي لذلك أن ألقتني في اليم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further reading says Moses’ mother and other enslaved Israelites raised him, so his upbringing was not Pharaoh’s favor; the author judges this less supported by the wording.
rows.anchor: أن الذي رباني أمي وغيرها من بني إسرائيل حيث استعبدتهم فأمرتهم فربوني فليست هذه التربية نعمة منك تمنها علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation treats the words as Moses’ admission that Pharaoh favored him by raising him while leaving him personally unenslaved.
rows.anchor: ذلك اعتراف منه عليه السلام بنعمة فرعون عليه والمعنى وتلك التربية نعمة منك تمنها علي أن عبدت بني إسرائيل وتركت تعبيدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author objects that the wording gives no evidence for the proposed addition, “and left me unenslaved.”
rows.anchor: لا دليل على ما قدره من قوله وتركت تعبيدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Pharaoh challenged Moses’ claim to be a messenger, he turned to the sender Moses identified as Lord of the worlds and questioned what that title meant, beginning a seven-verse exchange.
rows.anchor: بقوله { وما رب العالمين }؟ إلى تمام سبع آيات.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the pagans’ account, all things ultimately depend on one Necessary Being, without peer, whose reality is beyond delimitation, comprehension, or perception.
rows.anchor: يرون أن وجود الأشياء ينتهي إلى موجد واجب الوجود هو واحد لا شريك له في وجوب وجوده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They deem this supreme being unfit for worship because worship entails turning toward and apprehending its object.
rows.anchor: لا يجوز عبادته لأن العبادة نوع توجه إلى المعبود والتوجه إدراك.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Instead, they seek nearness to created, exalted luminous or fiery beings—angels, jinn, and purified human saints—who are absorbed in divinity.
rows.anchor: عدلوا عن عبادته والتقرب إليه إلى التقرب إلى أشياء من خلقه ذوي وجودات شريفة نورية أو نارية،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They worship such beings through idols to approach God and obtain intercession: angels transmit good, while jinn avert the evils issuing from them.
rows.anchor: وبالجملة كانوا يعبدونهم بعبادة أصنامهم ليقربوهم إلى الله زلفى ويشفعوا لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their deities each govern a universal affair, such as love, hatred, peace, war, or prosperity, or a particular sphere such as heaven, earth, or humanity.
rows.anchor: فإن كلا من هؤلاء المعبودين يرجع إليه تدبير أمر من أمور العالم الكلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Under this hierarchy, angels, jinn, and human saints govern their assigned worlds, while God is the deity of the gods and Lord of lords.
rows.anchor: إله عالم الآلهة وهو الله سبحانه فهو إله الآلهة ورب الأرباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If “Lord of the worlds” means a particular possible being, that being rules only its own created domain, not every world.
rows.anchor: لو أريد به بعض هذه الموجودات الشريفة الممكنة بأعيانهم فهو رب عالم من عوالم الخلقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the title means God, then on pagan premises he is Lord only of the world of gods, not all worlds; any other proposed referent has no intelligible instance.
rows.anchor: ولو أريد به الله سبحانه فهو رب عالم الأرباب وإله عالم الآلهة فقط دون جميع العالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s question asks what “Lord of the worlds” really is; he is both an idol-worshiping pagan and a claimant to divinity.
rows.anchor: سؤال منه عن حقيقة رب العالمين بيانه أن فرعون كان وثنيا يعبد الأصنام وهو مع ذلك يدعي الألوهية،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an supports Pharaoh’s idol worship and his claim to be the highest lord.
rows.anchor: ويذرك وآلهتك الأعراف 127

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author cites Pharaoh’s declaration “I am your highest lord” as evidence of his claim to divinity.
rows.anchor: فقال أنا ربكم الأعلى النازعات 24

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For pagans, a being can be a deity and lord while itself governed by a higher lord: lordship is independent management of one domain, compatible with contingency; only God has no lord above him.
rows.anchor: ولا منافاة عند الوثنية بين كون الشيء إلها ربا وبين كونه مربوب الرب آخر لأن الربوبية هو الاستقلال في تدبير شيء من العالم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pagan kings were treated as manifestations of divinity through authority, and worshiped like idol gods; Pharaoh’s subjects worshiped him as king of the Copts.
rows.anchor: وكان الملك عند الوثنية ظهورا من اللاهوت في بعض النفوس البشرية بالسلطة ونفوذ الحكم فكان يعبد الملوك كما يعبد أرباب الأصنام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hearing Moses and Aaron call themselves messengers of the Lord of the worlds, Pharaoh could not find a coherent referent: God rules only the gods, while other deities govern only particular worlds.
rows.anchor: فلما سمع من موسى وهارون قولهما { إنا رسول رب العالمين } تعجب منه إذ لم يعقل له معنى محصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh was not asking about God’s essence: as a pagan he already affirmed God’s existence and believed the divine essence could not be apprehended.
rows.anchor: لم يسأل عن حقيقة لله سبحانه فإنه لوثنيته كان معتقدا بوجوده مذعنا له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ answer completes an implied subject: the Lord is of the heavens, earth, and everything between them; their connected, unified governance indicates one governor to people of certainty through proof and experience.
rows.anchor: هو رب السماوات والأرض وما بينهما التي تدل بوجود التدبير فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A possible objection is that Pharaoh requested a conception of the title, whereas certainty is assent, and naming the heavens and earth only substitutes examples for “worlds.”
rows.anchor: فإن قلت لم يطلب فرعون من موسى عليه السلام إلا أن يعرفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author accepts that Pharaoh wanted a conception, but says Moses’ substitution points to the connection among the worlds and the unity of their governing order.
rows.anchor: لكن موسى بدل القول بوضع { السماوات والأرض وما بينهما } مكان العالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The condition “if you are certain” indicates that the certain affirm one governor of all the worlds; assent to one Lord entails some conception of him, since assent without conception is impossible.
rows.anchor: ليدل على أن أهل اليقين يصدقون من ذلك بوجود مدبر واحد لجميع العالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses identifies the Lord as the one whose lordship over all heavens, earth, and what lies between is affirmed by the certain when they observe unified governance.
rows.anchor: رب العالمين هو الذي يوقن الموقنون بربوبيته لجميع السماوات والأرض وما بينهما إذا نظروا إليها وشاهدوا وحدة التدبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Actual assent proves that God is apprehended and correctly conceived in some way, even though his essence cannot be grasped or encompassed in knowledge.
rows.anchor: الاحتجاج بتحقق التصديق على تحقق التصور قبله أقوى ما يمكن أن يحتج به على أنه تعالى مدرك بوجه ومتصور تصورا صحيحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer directs Pharaoh to what believers in certainty conceive of God; its proof establishes unity of lordship from unified governance, the point at issue against pagan co-lords.
rows.anchor: أن الذي أشير إليه من الحجة في الآية هو البرهان على توحيد الربوبية المأخوذ من وحدة التدبير

rows.speaker: ما ذكروا
rows.claim: Some commentators say Moses shifted from defining God’s essence by a delimiting definition to describing him through attributes, with createdness proving one necessary creator; the author rejects this as ineffective against pagans who already hold those premises.
rows.anchor: ما ذكروا أن العلم بحقيقة الذات لما كان ممتنعا عدل موسى عليه السلام عن تعريف الحقيقة بالحد إلى تعريفه تعالى بصفاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s question to his entourage means, “Will you not listen closely?” It expresses amazement that Moses claims a Lord’s message, then repeats the same title when asked what the Lord is.
rows.anchor: أي ألا تصغون إلى ما يقول موسى؟ والاستفهام للتعجيب يريد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh is using this performance to conceal the truth that had emerged from Moses’ argument about one governor over all worlds.
rows.anchor: وهذا تمويه منه عليهم يريد به الستر على الحق الذي لاح من كلام موسى عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the explanation that Pharaoh’s amazement means Moses was asked about God’s essence but answered only with an attribute: the question concerns the essence insofar as qualified.
rows.anchor: بان عدم سداد قولهم في تفسير هذا التعجيب إن مراده أني سألته عن الذات فأجاب بالصفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses did not define the essence by an attribute; he replaced “worlds” with “heavens and earth,” as though signaling that Pharaoh had not understood “worlds.”
rows.anchor: كأنه يومي إلى أن فرعون لم يفهم معنى العالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses gives a second answer because Pharaoh was misleading the audience: he specifies God’s lordship over human communities, present and past, since a “world” can mean a group of people or things.
rows.anchor: عدل ثانيا إلى ما يكون أصرح في المقصود فذكر ربوبيته تعالى لعالمي الإنسانية فإن العالم الجماعة من الناس أو الأشياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh was really defending his own claimed divinity, trying to deny that the Lord’s rule extends to him as part of the worlds, which would invalidate the rule of every lesser lord.
rows.anchor: فإن فرعون ما كان يدافع في الحقيقة إلا عن نفسه لما كان يدعي الألوهية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh had claimed to be the highest lord and told his chiefs that he knew no god for them besides himself.
rows.anchor: فقال أنا ربكم الأعلى النازعات 24

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author also recalls Pharaoh’s declaration that he knew no god for his people other than himself.
rows.anchor: يا أيها الملأ ما علمت لكم من إله غيري القصص 38

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ answer is that there is only one Lord of all worlds, who is therefore Pharaoh’s Lord too and the one who sent Moses to them.
rows.anchor: ليس في الوجود إلا رب واحد فيكون رب العالمين فهو ربكم وقد أرسلني إليكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ explicit identification of the Lord as ruler of present and past humanity defeats Pharaoh’s pretense that Moses merely repeated himself.
rows.anchor: هو رب عالمي الإنسانية من الحاضرين والماضين وبذلك تنقطع حيلته.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh calls Moses “your messenger” mockingly and distances himself from the message by addressing only his entourage.
rows.anchor: سمى موسى رسولا تهكما واستهزاء وأضافه إلى من حوله ترفعا من أن يكون رسولا إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s accusation of madness treats Moses’ explanation as incoherent: after being asked what the Lord of the worlds is, Moses first repeats the title and then calls him the Lord of them and their forefathers.
rows.anchor: كأنه يقول إنه لمجنون لما في كلامه من الاختلال الكاشف عن الاختلال في تعقله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “East” and “west” mean the directions where the sun and other luminous celestial bodies rise and set; everything between them spans the visible universe, equivalent to the heavens, earth, and what lies between.
rows.anchor: المراد بالمشرق جهة شروق الشمس وسائر الأجرام النيرة السماوية وطلوعها وبالمغرب الجهة التي تغرب فيها بحسب الحس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The east–west answer restates the first proof: sunrise and sunset, like the ends and middle between them, are connected aspects of one order requiring a single, continuous governor.
rows.anchor: إعادة المعنى الجواب الأول بتقرير آخر وهو مشتمل على ما اشتمل عليه من نكتة اتصال التدبير واتحاده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The link between present and past peoples likewise shows one human kind and one system of governance, hence one governor.
rows.anchor: كل أمة حاضرة لها ارتباط وجودي بالأمم الماضية ارتباط الأخلاف بالأسلاف فالنوع واحد والتدبير واحد فالمدبر واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By saying “if you reason” after Pharaoh mocked him and called him mad, Moses implies they lack understanding; sound reason would recognize his first answer as a sufficient proof of one Lord.
rows.anchor: إلى أنهم هم المحرومون من نعمة التعقل والتفقه ولو كانوا يعقلون لفهموا أن جوابه الأول ليس بتكرار غير مفيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse restates the first answer and proves one governor through unified governance; its account is clearer because sunrise and sunset are readily apparent.
rows.anchor: وأنه برهان على وحدة المدبر من طريق وحدة التدبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Moses’ story, the passage turns to Abraham’s momentous effort to affirm God’s oneness among idolaters: his pure innate disposition led him to reject them and defend truth, yet most of his people did not believe.
rows.anchor: إذ انتهض لتوحيد الله سبحانه بفطرته الزاكية الطاهرة من بين قومه المطبقين على عبادة الأصنام فتبرأ منهم ودافع عن الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to recite the account to the Arabs, especially Quraysh, matters because Abraham was their forefather and had established monotheism in the holy land and Hijaz with God’s support.
rows.anchor: فإن المطلوب تلاوته على مشركي العرب وعمدتهم قريش وإبراهيم هذا أبوهم وقد قام لنشر التوحيد وإقامة الدين الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s divinely supported, innate call is a sign for the Arab idolaters to learn from and to renounce idolatry as their forefather did.
rows.anchor: فلم يكن ذلك كله إلا عن دعوة من الفطرة وبعث من الله سبحانه ففي ذلك آية لله فليعتبروا به وليتبرءوا من دين الوثنية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account compresses Abraham’s separate debates with his father and his people into one dialogue, presenting their shared substance; the author compares it with the fuller accounts elsewhere.
rows.anchor: مخاصمته ومناظرته عليه السلام مع أبيه غير مخاصمته مع قومه واحتجاجه عليهم كما حكاه الله تعالى في سورة الأنعام وغيرها لكن البناء ها هنا على الإيجاز والاختصار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham asks “what do you worship?” as if ignorant, a debating tactic that makes opponents state their claim so he can hold them to it.
rows.anchor: سؤال عن الحقيقة بوضع نفسه موضع من لا يعرف شيئا من حقيقتها وسائر شؤونها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This debate occurred when Abraham first left his cave and entered his father’s and people’s society; having witnessed none of their practice before, he argued from pure, unspoiled innate disposition.
rows.anchor: كانت من إبراهيم أول ما خرج من كهفه ودخل في مجتمع أبيه وقومه ولم يكن شهد شيئا من ذلك قبل اليوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the reply, “ẓalla” means continued, “ʿukūf” means remaining with something, and the lām in “for them” gives a causal sense: they persist in devotion to idols for the idols’ sake.
rows.anchor: العكوف على الشيء ملازمته والإقامة عنده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An idol is a bodily object, made of metal, wood, or similar material and shaped to represent attributes of the being worshiped.
rows.anchor: والصنم جثة مأخوذة من فلز أو خشب أو غير ذلك على هيئة خاصة يمثل بها ما في المعبود من الصفات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worshipers of angels and jinn, who considered them immaterial spirits, used bodily forms to represent them because direct devotional attention to such spirits was difficult.
rows.anchor: ولما كان من الصعب عليهم التوجه العبادي إلى هذه الروحانيات باستحضارها للإدراك توسلوا إلى ذلك باتخاذ صور وتماثيل جسمانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Planet worshipers first worshiped planetary spirits and then their celestial bodies; because planets appeared and disappeared, they made idols representing their supposed powers over the elemental world, such as Venus for joy, Mars for bloodshed, and Mercury for knowledge.
rows.anchor: اتخذوا لها أصناما تمثل ما للكواكب من القوى الفعالة فيما دونها من عالم العناصر كالقوة الفاعلة للطرب والسرور والنشاط في الزهرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idols were made as images of a spiritual lord, but worshipers direct worship to the idol itself; even worship directed beyond it goes to a created being rather than God.
rows.anchor: الأصنام إنما اتخذت ليكون الواحد منها مرآة لرب الصنم من ملك أو جن أو إنسان غير أنهم يعبدون الصنم نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the claim that an idol is merely a qibla like the Kaʿba: Muslims face the qibla while worshiping God, whereas idolaters face and worship the idol; worship of its spirit would still be worship of a creature, not God.
rows.anchor: القبلة هي ما يستقبل في العبادة ولا يستقبل بالعبادة وهم يستقبلون الصنم في العبادة وبالعبادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham uses their admission that they worship idols against them: if the statues are the actual objects of worship, they must provide the intended benefit or protection, yet they cannot hear requests or answer the distressed.
rows.anchor: فإذ كانت مقصودة بالعبادة فمن الواجب أن يشتمل على ما هو الغرض المقصود منها من جلب نفع أو دفع ضر بالتوجه العبادي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s first objection is that worship expresses the worshiper’s need and humility and entails invocation; invocation requires the object to hear and know the request, which inert idols cannot do.
rows.anchor: العبادة تمثيل لذلة العابد وحاجته إلى المعبود فلا يخلو من دعاء من العابد للمعبود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His second objection is that worship seeks benefit or protection from harm, while idols have no power to confer benefit or repel injury.
rows.anchor: الناس إنما يعبدون الإله إما طمعا في خيره ونفعه وإما اتقاء من شره وضره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham frames both objections as questions to compel his audience to admit the idols cannot hear, benefit, or harm.
rows.anchor: وقد أوردهما في صورة الاستفهام ليضطرهم على الاعتراف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rather than answer the questions negatively and concede the idols’ impotence, Abraham’s people retreat to ancestor imitation as their only support for idolatry.
rows.anchor: لكنه لما كان ينتج خلاف ما هم عليه من الانتحال بالوثنية أضربوا عنه إلى التشبث بذيل التقليد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We found our fathers doing this” means they acted and worshiped as their fathers did; the phrasing emphasizes imitation of ritual forms without understanding anything beyond them.
rows.anchor: ففعلنا كما كانوا يفعلون وعبدناهم كما كانوا يعبدون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the debate exposed imitation as their only argument and showed idolatry false, Abraham disavows both the idols and their worshipers, declaring the idols enemies because they damage his religion and destroy his soul.
rows.anchor: لما انتهت محاجته مع أبيه وقومه إلى أن لا حجة لهم في عبادتهم الأصنام إلا تقليد آباءهم محضا تبرأ عليه السلام من آلهتهم ومن أنفسهم وآبائهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By naming the earliest forefathers, Abraham makes clear that he does not follow imitation and that historical precedence cannot invalidate truth or establish falsehood.
rows.anchor: وذكر آبائهم الأقدمين للدلالة على أنه لا يأخذ بالتقليد كما أخذوا وأن لا وقع عنده عليه السلام لتقدم العهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The animate pronoun for idols is used because worship is attributed to them, which implies awareness and intelligence; this usage is frequent in the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: لمكان نسبة العبادة إليها وهي تستلزم الشعور والعقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Except the Lord of the worlds” is a disconnected exception: it means that the Lord of the worlds is not an enemy to Abraham.
rows.anchor: أي لكن رب العالمين ليس كذلك.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham then describes the Lord with attributes that complete the proof: God is not his enemy but a merciful Lord who cares for him, grants every good, and wards off harm.
rows.anchor: وصفه بأوصاف تتم بها الحجة على أنه تعالى ليس عدوا له بل رب رحيم ذو عناية بحاله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the view that “who created me” begins an insignificant new passage, the author argues that Abraham begins with creation to infer that God also governs his affairs.
rows.anchor: استيناف من الكلام لا يعبأ به.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In gradual bodily existence, creation and governance cannot be separated; because God creates, he also manages, and the fāʾ in “then guides me” makes guidance follow from creation.
rows.anchor: لوضوح أن الخلق والتدبير لا ينفكان في هذه الموجودات الجسمانية التدريجية الوجود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unqualified “guides me” means guidance to all beneficial ends, worldly or otherworldly; its present tense conveys ongoing guidance from creation onward and forever.
rows.anchor: أن المراد به مطلق الهداية إلى المنافع دنيوية كانت أو أخرويه
